Python automation user-agent (python-requests / simple-salesforce) hitting Salesforce API at scale AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the Phase-4 execution pattern — long-running Python automation querying the Salesforce REST / Bulk API via the stolen Klue OAuth tokens. ReliaQuest specifically called out non-browser Python user-agents driving SOQL bulk queries against Account / Contact / Opportunity objects. Rationale: ReliaQuest's specific call-out: 'attackers generating OAuth tokens and using Python scripts to query Salesforce's API for extended periods'. The python-requests / simple-salesforce default user-agents are the standard SDK fingerprint — legit Klue Battlecards traffic uses its own UA string. Volume threshold (500/session) targets the bulk-pull behaviour from Phase-6 collection. Falcon empty because FDR doesn't carry Salesforce-side API telemetry.
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1213.003 T1119
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal data-engineering team running scheduled Python ETLs against Salesforce via Airflow / dbt / Fivetran
  • Marketing-ops Python scripts pulling Account/Contact data for analytics warehouses
  • Salesforce CLI tools that wrap python-requests (`sfdx`, salesforce-bulk libraries) used by admins
  • Backup tools like OwnBackup / Spanning that use Python SDKs under the hood
  • Customer-developed Heroku Connect jobs hitting their own org
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !has_any ("dataeng","etl","airflow","fivetran","heroku","backup")
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the top offending AccountDisplayName / SourceIP rows. Identify whether the principal is a service / integration user (suspect) or a real admin (likely BAU). Cross-check IPs against the four named Icarus IPs and the Klue published egress block. 2. Contain: if confirmed unauthorized, immediately revoke the connected app or service-user OAuth tokens in Salesforce Setup → OAuth Usage → Revoke; rotate the integration user credentials; force-expire all sessions; quarantine the source IP via Salesforce Network Access settings. 3. Hunt: enumerate which sObjects were queried by pulling Salesforce EventLogFile rows of type `API`, `RestApi`, and `BulkApi` for the session; sum result-set sizes to estimate exfiltration volume; check for follow-on extortion contact via EmailEvents looking for Session messenger IDs referencing the affected company.
let IcarusIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| where UserAgent has_any ("python-requests","simple-salesforce","python-urllib","Python/","aiohttp","httpx/")
| summarize ApiCalls = count(),
            DistinctObjects = dcount(ObjectName),
            DistinctActions = dcount(ActionType),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen  = max(Timestamp),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
            by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId
| where ApiCalls > 500 or IPs has_any (IcarusIPs)
| extend SessionDurationHrs = datetime_diff('minute', LastSeen, FirstSeen) / 60.0
| order by ApiCalls desc
let IcarusIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName has_any ("my.salesforce.com","force.com","salesforce.com")
| where RequestClientApplication has_any ("python-requests","simple-salesforce","python-urllib","Python/","aiohttp","httpx/")
| summarize ApiCalls = count(),
            BytesIn = sum(toint(ReceivedBytes)),
            BytesOut = sum(toint(SentBytes)),
            UserAgents = make_set(RequestClientApplication, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen  = max(TimeGenerated)
            by SourceIP, SourceUserName
| where ApiCalls > 500 or SourceIP in (IcarusIPs)
| extend SessionDurationHrs = datetime_diff('minute', LastSeen, FirstSeen) / 60.0
| order by ApiCalls desc

Endpoint or network egress to Icarus operator IPs (Klue Salesforce breach C2) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any inbound or outbound network connection between corporate endpoints / VPC infrastructure and the four operator IPs Icarus used during the Klue OAuth breach. Catches operator infrastructure reaching corporate Salesforce relay hosts, dev workstations, or any compromised pivot inside the perimeter. Rationale: Direct IOC hits on the four operator IPs cited in the kill-chain block's c2 and exfiltration phases. Endpoint, proxy, and VPC flow coverage in parallel since the same IPs could touch developer workstations (DeviceNetworkEvents / Falcon), proxy-fronted Salesforce relays (CommonSecurityLog), or AWS-hosted Salesforce Mulesoft adaptors (VPC flow).
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel ingestion sandboxes replaying IOCs from a feed
  • SOC analyst manually browsing the Icarus DLS / verifying IOCs from their workstation
  • Honeypot / deception infrastructure deliberately drawing attacker traffic
  • Tor exit node reuse: one of the four IPs being a Tor relay used by privacy-conscious users (unlikely on /32 operator IPs)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe")  // analyst IOC-validation browsing
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull DeviceNetworkEvents / Falcon NetworkConnectIP4 record — capture DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, and Timestamp. Determine whether the connection initiator is a user browser (likely IOC-validation), a service process (suspect), or a Salesforce integration daemon (high suspicion of pivot). 2. Contain: block all four IPs at the perimeter firewall, EDR network-isolation policy, and the corporate proxy. If the connection involved a service / non-browser process, isolate the host via Defender or Falcon Real-Time-Response and capture memory. 3. Hunt: pivot the InitiatingProcess SHA256 across DeviceProcessEvents for additional victims; check 30-day Salesforce CloudAppEvents for any session originating from the same DeviceName; review DNS logs for hostnames resolving to these IPs to catch domain-fronted variants.
let IcarusIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (IcarusIPs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, ActionType, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol,

| order by Timestamp desc

Inbound Icarus extortion email referencing Klue breach + Session messenger contact AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects inbound email containing the Icarus actor name + Session messaging-platform contact instruction targeting executive / security / legal mailboxes. Icarus deliberately steered victims to Session for ransom negotiations as a Tor-replacement OPSEC measure; combined keyword shape is high-fidelity. Rationale: Article kill-chain Phase-9 impact: 'pressure Klue and affected organizations to contact them through the Session messaging platform'. Huntress independently confirmed Session Messenger IDs as the actor's contact channel. The Icarus+Session+Klue tri-keyword shape is specific enough to keep noise low; Sigma omitted because the detection needs an OR across multiple fields and isn't a clean single-selection rule. Falcon empty (no email telemetry in FDR).
ATT&CKT1657 T1071.003
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal security awareness emails or threat-intel circulars discussing the Icarus / Klue incident
  • News-digest emails (Bleeping Computer, KrebsOnSecurity, Risky.Biz) covering the breach
  • Vendor advisories from Huntress / ReliaQuest / CrowdStrike about the campaign
  • Penetration-test post-engagement reports referencing the Icarus group as a TTP example
  • Internal IR communications between security team mailboxes about the breach
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !has_any ("huntress.com","reliaquest.com","crowdstrike.com","bleepingcomputer.com","sans.org")
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the email's NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, headers, and full body. Verify AuthenticationDetails (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) — extortion email typically fails or comes from a one-shot domain. If the recipient is a named executive (CEO/CFO/General Counsel) and the body contains a specific Session ID + ransom demand, escalate immediately. 2. Contain: purge the message tenant-wide via Defender → Email entity → Submit-and-purge; block the sender domain and any URLs at Defender Safe Links; notify the recipient out-of-band (NOT email reply) that the message is part of a known extortion campaign. 3. Hunt: search 90d of EmailEvents for the same SenderFromDomain and Session contact IDs across the org; correlate with Salesforce CloudAppEvents to confirm whether the recipient's company was actually breached; review UrlClickEvents for any user who clicked an Icarus DLS link.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where Subject has_any ("Icarus","Klue breach","Klue.com","Salesforce data","data leak") 
    or AdditionalFields has_any ("Icarus","Session Messenger","sessionid")
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | summarize Urls = make_set(Url, 10), Domains = make_set(UrlDomain, 10) by NetworkMessageId
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| extend MentionsSession = tostring(AdditionalFields) has "Session" or tostring(Urls) has "getsession.org"
| where MentionsSession or Subject has "Icarus"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails, Urls, Domains
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity

   or EventData has_any ("Icarus","Session Messenger","getsession.org")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenRemote Manager bulk alarm DELETE endpoint hit (GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf) AIExploitation Medium
Detects HTTP DELETE requests to OpenRemote Manager's vulnerable bulk-alarm endpoint /api/{realm}/alarm. The article's PoC sends `DELETE /api/smartcity/alarm` with a JSON array body of alarm IDs; the underlying removeAlarms() method has no per-alarm realm check, so any DELETE matching this path shape against an OpenRemote Manager build < 1.24.2 is the literal exploitation surface. Rationale: Targets the exact endpoint shape from the article PoC `DELETE /api/smartcity/alarm`. The realm segment is extracted from the URL so downstream rules can join to the authenticated user's home realm. Status filter 200/204 narrows to successful deletes (skips the 404 enumeration noise). Cross-checked against GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf advisory text. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tenant administrator performing legitimate alarm hygiene
  • Scheduled retention job calling the bulk-delete API
  • QA/staging environment resetting fixtures
  • SOAR playbook that auto-clears alarms after triage
  • Mobile app sync clearing acknowledged alarms
Suppression filter
| where csUsername !in~ ("alarm-retention-svc", "openremote-backup-svc", "soar-cleanup")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the request body (from application or WAF logs) and count alarm IDs; from auth/session logs determine the caller's home realm and compare to the realm in the URL path. Confirm OpenRemote Manager version — anything < 1.24.2 is vulnerable. 2) Contain: revoke caller's session/token, disable the account, snapshot the SentAlarm table and restore from backup if IDs span multiple realms. Push the upgrade to 1.24.2+. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same source IP / account for prior /api/*/alarm DELETEs with 4xx responses (boundary probing) and any other bulk endpoints (assets, datapoints, attributes) that may share the same missing-authorization defect.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod =~ "DELETE"
| where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)^/api/[^/]+/alarm$"
| where scStatus in ("200","204")
| extend Realm = extract(@"(?i)/api/([^/]+)/alarm", 1, csUriStem)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, csUsername, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, Realm, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: OpenRemote Manager Bulk Alarm Delete Endpoint Access (GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf)
id: 7b3a5e02-1f44-4a8b-9c2c-3a0b1de4f9c1

| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="DELETE" Web.url="*/api/*/alarm" Web.status IN (200,204) by _time, Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.status span=1m | rename Web.* as * | rex field=url "/api/(?<realm>[^/]+)/alarm$" | where isnotnull(realm) | stats count by _time, src, user, dest, realm, status
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="DELETE" Web.url="*/api/*/alarm" Web.status IN (200,204) by _time, Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.status span=1m | rename Web.* as * | rex field=url "/api/(?<realm>[^/]+)/alarm$" | where isnotnull(realm) | stats count by _time, src, user, dest, realm, status
Bulk alarm DELETE volume anomaly — non-admin OpenRemote user AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a single authenticated user issuing >=20 DELETE requests to /api/*/alarm within a 10-minute window. Article emphasises bulk deletion as the impact vector; normal users should not approach this volume — only successful IDOR exploitation or account compromise produces this shape. Rationale: Article quotes the PoC body `[1174,1173, 1180]` and frames the impact as bulk destruction of safety-critical alarms; even a small array per request quickly stacks into 20+ deletes when an attacker chains enumeration with exploitation. Threshold is per (user, 10m bin) so legitimate single-shot admin cleanups don't trip. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf
ATT&CKT1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Retention service account purging acknowledged alarms in bulk
  • Tenant admin doing one-off mass cleanup after a noisy false-positive storm
  • Migration/decommission tooling clearing alarms on a sunset realm
  • Load/perf test against the alarm API in a non-prod tenant
Suppression filter
| where csUsername !in~ ("alarm-retention-svc", "openremote-backup-svc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: list the (user, src IP, realm) tuples and decide if the user is a known retention service or a tenant admin; pull a sample of the DELETE bodies and check whether IDs span multiple realms (the IDOR signature). 2) Contain: revoke session/API tokens for the user, disable the account, then snapshot the SentAlarm table; if realm-spanning IDs are confirmed, restore safety-critical alarms from backup and notify affected tenants. 3) Hunt: search prior 24h for the same caller hitting other openremote bulk endpoints (assets, datapoints, attributes) and for any 200 responses to /api/*/alarm preceded by 401/403 (probe-then-exploit).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod =~ "DELETE"
| where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)^/api/[^/]+/alarm$"
| where scStatus in ("200","204")
| summarize DeleteCount = count(), Realms = make_set(extract(@"(?i)/api/([^/]+)/alarm", 1, csUriStem)), FirstDelete = min(TimeGenerated), LastDelete = max(TimeGenerated), SrcIPs = make_set(cIP), UA = make_set(csUserAgent)
          by bin(TimeGenerated, 10m), csUsername, Computer
| where DeleteCount >= 20
| order by DeleteCount desc

WEB

| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="DELETE" Web.url="*/api/*/alarm" Web.status IN (200,204) by _time, Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest span=10m | rename Web.* as * | where count >= 20 | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="DELETE" Web.url="*/api/*/alarm" Web.status IN (200,204) by _time, Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest span=10m | rename Web.* as * | where count >= 20 | sort - count
OpenRemote alarm DELETE 401/403 probe burst followed by 200/204 success AIReconnaissance High
Detects a user generating >=2 authorization-failed DELETEs against /api/*/alarm immediately followed by >=3 successful DELETEs to the same endpoint within 5 minutes — the boundary-probing shape an IDOR exploiter produces while mapping which realms / IDs they can reach. Rationale: Article's attack-vector section explicitly describes the attacker enumerating across realms and observing response codes before issuing the destructive bulk delete. Sequencing fail-then-succeed within 5 minutes captures the probe-then-exploit signal that distinguishes targeted IDOR abuse from a benign admin who only ever sees 200s. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf
ATT&CKT1190 T1087
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User loses session mid-cleanup, re-authenticates, resumes deletes (legit fail→success)
  • Race against a token-refresh causing transient 401s
  • Frontend SPA retrying after a CSRF/XSRF token rotation
  • SOAR retrying a deletion playbook after an upstream auth glitch
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate the realms in csUriStem across the 5-minute window — multiple distinct realm names in URL path is the strongest IDOR indicator. Check whether the failures cluster on realms not assigned to the user. 2) Contain: revoke session/API tokens, disable the account, and force a tenant-wide password reset if the source IP matches multiple compromised users. Patch to OpenRemote Manager >= 1.24.2. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP / user-agent across other GET/POST/PUT verbs against /api/*/alarm and adjacent resources (assets, datapoints) to scope the recon footprint.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod =~ "DELETE"
| where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)^/api/[^/]+/alarm$"
| summarize Failures = countif(scStatus in ("401","403")),
            Successes = countif(scStatus in ("200","204")),
            FirstFailure = minif(TimeGenerated, scStatus in ("401","403")),
            FirstSuccess = minif(TimeGenerated, scStatus in ("200","204")),
            TargetedRealms = make_set(extract(@"(?i)/api/([^/]+)/alarm", 1, csUriStem)),
            SrcIPs = make_set(cIP)
          by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m), csUsername
| where Failures >= 2 and Successes >= 3 and FirstSuccess > FirstFailure
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenRemote alarm endpoint enumeration with realm-switching AIReconnaissance High
Detects a single user issuing repeated DELETEs to /api/*/alarm where the realm component of the URL path alternates between two or more distinct realms within 10 minutes. Article notes alarm IDs are sequential @GeneratedValue Longs and that an attacker can target arbitrary realms; multi-realm DELETE bursts from one account map to the cross-tenant enumeration phase of the exploit. Rationale: Article's PoC table shows two realms (tenant-a, tenant-b) and explicitly describes the attacker as a user in one realm targeting alarm IDs belonging to another. Counting distinct realm path segments per user per 10-minute bin captures the cross-tenant pivot regardless of whether the IDs themselves are enumerable from access logs. Langflow vulnerable to CVE-2026-55447 (BaseFileComponent symlink RCE, < 1.9.2) AIWeaponization High
Inventory pivot that surfaces every host running a Langflow version vulnerable to CVE-2026-55447 — the BaseFileComponent tar-symlink-traversal flaw fixed in 1.9.2 via PR #12945. Patch surface management before behavioural hunts, since the file-component ingest path is the only attack precondition. Rationale: Article gives a single concrete fix version (1.9.2) and CVE id (CVE-2026-55447) — TVM-grade inventory is the cheapest, highest-confidence first move before behavioural hunts. Cross-checked against IBM security bulletin describing the same BaseFileComponent path traversal mechanism. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/7273426 • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/pull/12945
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow dev/test instances kept on older versions intentionally pinned in a sandbox
  • TVM scan reporting the parent langflow-base package version but actual deployment is langflow CLI which pins differently
  • Containerised Langflow where TVM reads host OS rather than container image
  • Air-gapped lab installs with no external file ingest reachable
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm Langflow version with `pip show langflow` or the container image tag/digest; cross-check against the 1.9.2 fix version in PR #12945. Identify which BaseFileComponent-derived nodes (Read File, Docling, Unstructured, NvidiaIngest, VideoFile) are wired to user-reachable flows. 2) Contain — block /api/v1/files and /api/v2/files at the ingress (NetSec WAF) until upgraded; if Langflow is internet-exposed and unpatched, isolate the host. Pre-emptively rotate the Langflow secret_key file (`~/.langflow/secret_key` or `$LANGFLOW_CONFIG_DIR/secret_key`) so any pre-existing leaked JWT-signing key is invalidated. 3) Hunt — pivot to UC2 (file-credential touches) and UC3 (Python Interpreter shell spawns) on the same DeviceId list to see if exploitation already occurred.

| where CveId =~ "CVE-2026-55447"
| join kind=leftouter (

Langflow worker reads JWT secret_key or system credentials (CVE-2026-55447 symlink-traversal) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the literal credential-access step of CVE-2026-55447: a Langflow ingest worker (uvicorn/gunicorn/python invoking the langflow or lfx package) touches `~/.langflow/secret_key`, SSH private keys, AWS credentials, kube/docker configs or `/etc/shadow` — the symlink-traversal payload in `BaseFileComponent._unpack_bundle` resolves to one of these targets when an attacker uploads a crafted tar. Rationale: Targets the article's literal step 1 of the exploit chain: 'Upload a file that directs the node to read Langflow's secret_key file containing the JWT token secret.' The path `~/.langflow/secret_key` is the canonical Langflow JWT-signing key location, and the article names this file as the exfiltration target. Process pivots use the literal package strings (langflow, lfx, base_file, _unpack_bundle) from the article body's path `langflow/src/lfx/src/lfx/base/data/base_file.py`. Cross-checked against IBM advisory which independently confirms credential-file read as the impact. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/7273426 • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/pull/12945
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1083 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow process reading its own secret_key at worker startup (legitimate, happens once per boot)
  • Site-packages re-install touching files under Langflow config dir during pip upgrade
  • Backup agent running as the langflow service account reading /.ssh or /.aws as part of a scheduled snapshot
  • Container init script copying credentials into /.aws on first boot
  • Custom Langflow component that legitimately reads ~/.aws/credentials for cloud LLM auth (Bedrock, Vertex)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("systemd","init","docker-init","tini")
| where not (FolderPath has "/.langflow/secret_key" and Timestamp < InitiatingProcessCreationTime + 60s)
Response runbook
1) Triage — capture the InitiatingProcessId and confirm the timing isn't process-startup-correlated; pull DeviceProcessEvents for the same PID and check whether the parent is uvicorn/gunicorn handling an HTTP request vs the langflow CLI booting. Identify the upstream upload by joining to web/proxy logs by client IP. 2) Contain — rotate `~/.langflow/secret_key` (this invalidates all live JWTs, forcing re-auth); revoke API tokens; disable the file-ingest flow until the host is upgraded to Langflow ≥ 1.9.2. If SSH keys / AWS creds were touched, rotate those too. 3) Hunt — pivot to UC3 (Langflow worker spawning shells) on the same DeviceId for the following 24h; review files uploaded to /api/v1/files for tar/tgz content type; check whether any Python Interpreter node was added to a flow recently in the Langflow audit log.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow","lfx","base_file","_unpack_bundle")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.langflow/secret_key","/.ssh/","/.aws/","/.kube/","/.docker/","/root/","/etc/shadow","/etc/passwd")
   or FileName in~ ("secret_key","id_rsa","id_ed25519","id_ecdsa","credentials","kubeconfig","shadow")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessId, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow","lfx","base_file","_unpack_bundle")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.langflow/secret_key","/.ssh/","/.aws/","/.kube/","/.docker/","/root/","/etc/shadow")
   or TargetFileName in~ ("secret_key","id_rsa","id_ed25519","credentials","kubeconfig","shadow")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, DvcAction, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow Python worker spawns shell or network tool (CVE-2026-55447 Python Interpreter RCE) AIInstallation High
Hunts the article's final step: 'create a new flow with Python Interpreter node, fill it with arbitrary Python code and execute it.' Once the attacker has forged a JWT using the leaked secret_key, the Python Interpreter node becomes an RCE primitive — the langflow worker spawns shells, curl/wget, reverse-shell builtins, or chmod/base64 on tmp payloads, all under the langflow uvicorn/gunicorn parent. Rationale: Directly maps to the article's step 4: 'Code execution is then trivial — simply create a new flow with Python Interpreter node, fill it with arbitrary Python code and execute it.' The parent-process pivot (uvicorn/gunicorn/python with the literal package strings `langflow` and `lfx` from the article's source path `langflow/src/lfx/src/lfx/base/data/base_file.py`) plus the child binary set + reverse-shell command-line indicators give high-fidelity coverage of the post-RCE behavioural footprint. Cross-checked against IBM advisory and PR #12945, which confirm the RCE is reached via the Python Interpreter node downstream of credential theft. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/7273426 • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/pull/12945
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow flows that legitimately use a Shell Tool / Python Subprocess component for an internal data-pipeline use case
  • Container start scripts spawned by gunicorn master under healthcheck patterns
  • Developer running `langflow run` interactively from a shell who then opens another terminal via the same worker (uncommon but possible in dev)
  • wait-for-it.sh or dockerize-style init scripts wrapped around langflow startup that exec /bin/sh briefly
  • curl/wget invoked by Langflow's update-checker telemetry code path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("healthcheck","wait-for-it","dockerize","langflow-update-check")
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("/usr/local/bin/healthcheck","wait-for-it.sh","curl --fail http://127.0.0.1")
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the full process tree (ParentCmd, ChildCmd, grand-parent) for the InitiatingProcessId; confirm the child binary or command line matches a reverse-shell or downloader pattern, not a benign component. Cross-reference the host's Langflow version against UC1 — if <1.9.2, treat as live exploitation. 2) Contain — kill the offending child PID and quarantine the Langflow worker; rotate `~/.langflow/secret_key`; force all Langflow users to re-authenticate; block egress IPs reached by the child curl/wget at the firewall. 3) Hunt — pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on the same DeviceId/PID for outbound public IPs in the last 24h; check `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, `/etc/cron.d/*`, `/etc/systemd/system/*.service` and `~/.bashrc` for persistence drops; review Langflow flow-create audit entries for newly-added Python Interpreter nodes by accounts that don't normally author flows.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow","lfx","python_interpreter")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","perl","ruby","node","busybox","chmod","base64")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","python -c","curl http","wget http","chmod +x /tmp/","/tmp/.","nohup ","base64 -d")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, InitiatingProcessId, ProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow","lfx","python_interpreter")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/perl","/ruby","/node","/busybox","/chmod","/base64")
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","python -c","curl http","wget http","chmod +x /tmp/","/tmp/.","nohup ","base64 -d")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hunts POST requests to Langflow's vulnerable /api/v1/responses endpoint. Per the GHSA, any authenticated POST here can execute another user's flow when the `model` body field is set to a victim flow UUID. Surface every hit so an analyst can baseline who legitimately calls the endpoint. Rationale: Article literally embeds the vulnerable path /api/v1/responses, the POST method, and the default localhost:7860 PoC. Sigma rule is single-event shape (one selection on method+URI). Defender query limited to port-7860 pivot because URL path lives in the HTTP payload, not network-layer telemetry — noted in the query comment.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow users invoking their own flows via the responses API
  • Internal automation / CI pipelines running flows via stored x-api-key
  • Langflow's own web UI calling the endpoint when a user hits 'Run' on a flow they own
  • Health-check / monitoring probes hitting the endpoint after upgrade
  • Loadtest / pre-prod traffic during Langflow deployment validation
Suppression filter
| where SrcUsername !in ("langflow-healthcheck", "langflow-ci")
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !startswith "langflow-internal/"
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the requesting principal (x-api-key fingerprint, source IP, user-agent). Pull all POSTs from same src in the surrounding 30 min and extract the `model` JSON field from any request bodies you have captured. 2. Contain: if the Langflow instance is < 1.9.1, schedule emergency upgrade to 1.9.1+ and rotate ALL active API keys (the IDOR means any compromised key could have touched other tenants' flows). Block the source IP at the WAF if external. 3. Hunt: pivot on the API key to Langflow's own flow execution audit log — list every distinct flow_id it executed, then cross-check against the flow_owner_id table for non-owner matches. Pull the inputs/outputs of those flow executions to assess data exposure.
// Defender DeviceNetworkEvents can only see the L4 connection (port 7860 default), not the URL path. Use this as a coarse pivot to find hosts talking to Langflow; correlate with reverse-proxy logs for path visibility.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 7860 or RemoteUrl has "/api/v1/responses"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess", "InboundConnectionAccepted")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url contains "/api/v1/responses"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow IDOR enumeration — single-source fan-out POSTing /api/v1/responses AIActions on Objectives High
Detects systematic enumeration of victim flow UUIDs via the vulnerable IDOR endpoint. A legitimate user almost never POSTs >20 distinct calls to /api/v1/responses in 5 minutes; that volume is consistent with scripted UUID brute-forcing or wholesale flow harvesting. Rationale: Threshold (>20 in 5 min) implements the reviewer's UC_3_2 enumeration hypothesis. Article describes the PoC using a single curl POST per flow_id, so scraping every flow in a tenant means many sequential POSTs — exactly what this catches. Sigma omitted because aggregation/threshold logic falls outside Sigma's single-event model.
ATT&CKT1213 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Loadtest hitting Langflow API during pre-prod validation
  • Legitimate batch job replaying many flows for owner's own dataset processing
  • Langflow internal UI making polling/streaming calls (legitimate UI behavior should be allow-listed by user-agent)
  • API gateway retries during transient backend failures
  • Penetration tester running an authorized assessment
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.0/8 internal CI subnet", "<approved pentest CIDR>")
| where SrcUsername !in ("langflow-batch-svc", "langflow-loadtest")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the source IP and authenticated principal. Cross-check against pen-test calendar and approved automation list. Pull surrounding HTTP traffic to confirm rapid sequential POSTs (not random spread). 2. Contain: invalidate the offending x-api-key immediately, block source IP at the perimeter if external, and put the Langflow instance into maintenance mode if exfil volume looks significant. 3. Hunt: list every distinct flow_id touched by the principal in the last 30 days (from app logs / web bodies if captured); identify which flow owners need notification; check for outbound large-byte responses from Langflow to suspicious destinations indicating bulk data harvesting via executed flows.
// Defender lacks URL-path visibility for inbound web requests; this approximates by counting connections per source to Langflow's default port 7860.

| where RequestCount > 20
| order by RequestCount desc

Langflow CVE-2026-55255 vulnerable asset exposure (versions < 1.9.1) AIReconnaissance High
Identifies hosts running Langflow versions affected by CVE-2026-55255 (any version below 1.9.1). Prioritises internet-facing instances for emergency patching since the IDOR requires only valid authentication and the fix is a single minor version bump. Rationale: Article gives the exact CVE (CVE-2026-55255) and exact fix version (1.9.1) — perfect inputs for vuln-management table queries. DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities is the canonical Defender/Sentinel table for CVE-keyed asset exposure. Internet-facing prioritisation via DeviceInfo join since this exploit only needs auth.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already scheduled for patching in the current maintenance window
  • Isolated dev/test Langflow instances without production data
  • False inventory matches from generic Python package scanning where 'langflow' is a transitive dependency unused at runtime
  • Hosts with a compensating WAF rule already blocking /api/v1/responses
  • Air-gapped instances with no authenticated user population to abuse
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareName =~ "langflow"
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "1.9.1" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "1.9.2" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "1.10" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "2."
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm Langflow version on the host (`pip show langflow` or container image tag). Rule out false matches from inactive Python envs. Check internet exposure via DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing or external attack-surface tooling. 2. Contain: upgrade to Langflow 1.9.1+ (PR #12832 merged 2026-04-22). If immediate patch impossible, restrict /api/v1/responses at the reverse proxy (require additional auth header or block externally) and rotate all Langflow API keys. 3. Hunt: pivot to the web log UCs above to retro-actively look for IDOR exploitation against this host's pre-patch window; check Langflow application audit logs for any cross-ownership flow executions.

Langflow IDOR successful exploitation — HTTP 200 on /api/v1/responses AIActions on Objectives Medium
Surfaces successful (HTTP 200) POST executions of /api/v1/responses for analyst triage. Pre-1.9.1, a 200 means a flow ran; pairing this with Langflow's user→flow ownership map (joined out-of-band) lets you confirm whether the executing principal owned the flow. Used post-incident or when assessing whether known enumeration attempts actually succeeded. Rationale: Article confirms a successful exploit returns 200 OK (PoC: 'Returns 200 and executes the victim's flow'). Article also tells us the fix returns 404 for cross-user lookups, so post-patch this query naturally collapses to legitimate-only traffic. CloudWatch query included for ALB-fronted Langflow deployments — common AWS hosting shape. Cross-ownership confirmation requires Langflow's own flow ownership table, noted inline.
ATT&CKT1213
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Flow owners legitimately running their own flows (the dominant FP source)
  • Approved internal automation under service-account API keys
  • Langflow web UI's own Run button hitting the endpoint
  • API gateway health checks that intentionally exercise the endpoint
  • Post-patch traffic on 1.9.1+ (which returns 404 for IDOR attempts but 200 for legitimate runs)
Response runbook
1. Triage: extract the API key fingerprint and SrcUsername from the hit. Look up the request body (if captured at WAF/APM layer) for the `model` field — that's the targeted flow UUID. 2. Contain: out-of-band, query Langflow's database (`SELECT user_id FROM flow WHERE id = '<flow_uuid>'`) and compare against the authenticated principal. If mismatch, revoke the API key immediately, force-rotate all keys for the abused tenant, and notify the flow owner that their flow logic + any flow secrets may be compromised. 3. Hunt: list every distinct flow_uuid touched by the offending principal in the last 30d (from app logs/body captures); for each non-owned hit, retrieve the flow's response payloads to estimate data exposure scope.
// Defender lacks HTTP response code visibility for inbound traffic; this detection requires web-layer telemetry. Use Sentinel ImWebSession or W3CIISLog instead.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url contains "/api/v1/responses"
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| summarize SuccessfulRuns = count(), FirstRun = min(TimeGenerated), LastRun = max(TimeGenerated), UAs = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 5) by SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname
// Out-of-band: join SrcUsername (or API-key fingerprint) against Langflow's flow-ownership table; rows where the executing principal does not own the touched flow are confirmed IDOR exploitation.
| order by SuccessfulRuns desc

id: e8d4f1a2-9c3b-4e7d-8f5a-2b1c6d9e4f7a
description: Detects successful (HTTP 200) POST execution of Langflow's /api/v1/responses endpoint, the IDOR sink in CVE-2026-55255. Pair with out-of-band ownership join to confirm cross-user flow execution.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

  selection:

    sc-status: 200
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Owner legitimately executing their own flow via the API
  - Internal automation under approved service-account API keys
level: medium
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:apache.access OR source:web OR source:aws.alb) @http.method:POST @http.url_details.path:/api/v1/responses @http.status_code:200
# log group: /aws/applicationelb (set to whichever ALB fronts your Langflow service)
fields @timestamp, client_ip, request_url, request_verb, elb_status_code, user_agent, target_status_code
| filter request_verb = "POST"
      and request_url like /\/api\/v1\/responses/
      and elb_status_code = 200
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 200

``` Analyst: join `user` against the Langflow flow-ownership lookup (sourcetype=langflow:flow_owners) on the `model` body field to confirm cross-ownership. ```

Langflow flow execution by non-owner (post-IDOR confirmation) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts Langflow's own application audit log for flow execution events where the executing principal's user_id does not match the flow's owner user_id. This is the highest-fidelity signal for confirmed CVE-2026-55255 exploitation — the IDOR's literal symptom, observed from the application rather than the network. Rationale: Article explicitly states the IDOR allows attackers to 'execute any flow belonging to another user' — making executor_user_id != flow_owner_user_id the literal indicator of exploitation. Requires Langflow audit log ingestion (custom log table); query shapes target the canonical fields any Langflow audit pipeline would emit. Defender XDR has no path for these app logs so left noted-empty.
ATT&CKT1648 T1213
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Shared / team flows where multiple users have been granted execution rights outside the simple owner field (check if Langflow tenant has a sharing model beyond owner_id)
  • Admin or impersonation features where staff legitimately run flows on a user's behalf
  • Service-account principals that are designed to run all tenants' flows (e.g. scheduled job runner)
  • Migration/restore events where flow_owner_user_id was changed and historic runs look cross-owner in retrospect
  • Post-patch (1.9.1+) the IDOR is closed so genuine cross-owner runs should drop to zero — sustained hits post-patch are likely legitimate admin/impersonation, not exploitation
Suppression filter
| where executor_user_id_s !in ("langflow-admin-svc", "langflow-scheduler-svc", "langflow-impersonation-svc")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm Langflow version on the host. If < 1.9.1 and audit log shows cross-owner executions, treat as confirmed IDOR exploitation. Extract the API key fingerprint mapped to executor_user_id and the list of victim flow_ids. 2. Contain: revoke the offending API key, force key rotation for every victim tenant, take Langflow offline if exploitation is broad, and upgrade to 1.9.1+ immediately. Notify each victim flow owner that their flow may have been executed and that the flow's secrets (LLM API keys, DB creds, etc. embedded in flow definitions) should be rotated. 3. Hunt: for each (executor, victim_flow) pair, pull the actual flow inputs and outputs from Langflow's execution history to scope data exposure. Look for the executor's earlier enumeration via UC2 above to determine the discovery method.
// Defender XDR has no native ingestion path for Langflow application audit logs. Use Sentinel custom-log table or Splunk sourcetype=langflow:audit instead.
// Assumes Langflow audit logs are ingested into a custom table named Langflow_Audit_CL with fields executor_user_id_s, flow_id_g, flow_owner_user_id_s, event_type_s, src_ip_s.
Langflow_Audit_CL
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where event_type_s =~ "flow_execution"
| where isnotempty(executor_user_id_s) and isnotempty(flow_owner_user_id_s)
| where executor_user_id_s != flow_owner_user_id_s
| summarize CrossOwnerRuns = count(), FirstRun = min(TimeGenerated), LastRun = max(TimeGenerated), DistinctVictimFlows = dcount(flow_id_g), VictimOwners = make_set(flow_owner_user_id_s, 25) by executor_user_id_s, src_ip_s
| order by CrossOwnerRuns desc
source:langflow @event.type:flow_execution @executor.user_id:* @flow.owner.user_id:* -@executor.user_id:@flow.owner.user_id
# log group: /aws/lambda/langflow OR your Langflow application log group (e.g. /aws/ecs/langflow)
fields @timestamp, executor_user_id, flow_id, flow_owner_user_id, event_type, src_ip
| filter event_type = "flow_execution"
      and ispresent(executor_user_id)
      and ispresent(flow_owner_user_id)
      and executor_user_id != flow_owner_user_id
| stats count(*) as cross_owner_runs, count_distinct(flow_id) as victim_flows by executor_user_id, src_ip
| sort cross_owner_runs desc
| limit 100
APPLICATION
sourcetype=langflow:audit event_type=flow_execution
| eval is_cross_owner=if(executor_user_id!=flow_owner_user_id AND isnotnull(flow_owner_user_id) AND isnotnull(executor_user_id), 1, 0)
| where is_cross_owner=1
| stats count min(_time) as firstRun max(_time) as lastRun dc(flow_id) as distinct_victim_flows values(flow_owner_user_id) as victim_owners by executor_user_id, src_ip
| convert ctime(firstRun) ctime(lastRun)
| sort - count
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.

Inbound request to Craft CMS /actions/app/resource-js (CVE-2026-55791 trigger) AIDelivery Low
Surfaces every hit on the vulnerable Craft CMS resource-js proxy endpoint. This endpoint is the sole entry point for CVE-2026-55791 SSRF + JS-injection chain when trustedHosts is the default 'any'. Hunting query — analyst pivots on Host header, source IP, and response Content-Type to spot poisoning. Rationale: Pivots on the exact endpoint named in the GHSA (/actions/app/resource-js). HttpHostName is projected so analysts can spot Host/X-Forwarded-Host poisoning manually; production tuning should compare it against the org's canonical hostname. Cross-checked against: • https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10338 • https://dailycve.com/craft-cms-ssrf-via-host-header-cvenot-specified-critical/
ATT&CKT1190 T1659

  • Search-engine crawlers (Googlebot, Bingbot) requesting the resource

| where not (HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("Googlebot", "bingbot", "UptimeRobot", "Pingdom", "DataDog", "NewRelic")) and not (SrcIpAddr startswith "10." or SrcIpAddr startswith "192.168." or SrcIpAddr startswith "172.16.")

1) Triage: pull a sample of recent hits and inspect the Host header / X-Forwarded-Host (if logged by your WAF) — anything other than the canonical FQDN is a poisoning attempt. Check the SrcIpAddr against threat-intel and validate whether it's an internal monitor. 2) Contain: if poisoning is confirmed, purge any CDN/Varnish cache entries for /actions/app/resource-js, block the source IP at the edge, and immediately upgrade Craft to 4.17.9 / 5.9.15 (or set assetManager.cacheSourcePaths=true and trustedHosts to your FQDN). 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 (outbound SSRF) and UC3 (plugin install) using the same SrcIpAddr and a ±10 minute window to determine if the chain progressed beyond probing.

| where Url has "/actions/app/resource-js"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

SSRF outbound from Craft CMS web tier within seconds of /actions/app/resource-js request AICommand & Control High
Correlates an inbound hit on the vulnerable resource-js endpoint with an outbound HTTP(S) connection initiated by the web-server / PHP process to a non-RFC1918 destination within 30s. This is the high-fidelity signature of the SSRF: Guzzle (with ALLOW_REDIRECTS=true) fetching attacker-controlled JS. Rationale: Maps directly to the article's described chain: 'forcing the backend Guzzle client to fetch a malicious payload from an attacker-controlled server'. Joining the inbound /actions/app/resource-js request with an outbound web-tier connection within 30s eliminates 99% of background egress noise and produces a high-fidelity SSRF artefact. ALLOW_REDIRECTS=true (article §2B) means Guzzle will follow redirects, so any non-RFC1918 destination from the web process is the signal. Cross-checked against: • https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10338 • https://dailycve.com/craft-cms-ssrf-via-host-header-cvenot-specified-critical/

| where RemoteIPType == "Public"

Craft CMS Control Panel plugin install POST from non-baseline source (CVE-2026-55791 session-riding RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects the terminal RCE step of the CVE-2026-55791 chain: a POST to /admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin triggered by attacker JavaScript that stole window.Craft.csrfTokenValue from a poisoned cache entry. Alerts when the request originates from a source IP that has not historically performed admin actions. Rationale: Article §3 explicitly walks through the malicious JS extracting window.Craft.csrfTokenValue and POSTing to /admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin. Hard-coded endpoint is a high-fidelity pivot. The anti-join against a 30-day baseline of admin install posts strips out legitimate admins so any new SrcIpAddr is investigation-worthy. Cross-checked against: • https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10338
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190 T1548.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • New admin user installing a plugin from a previously-unseen home IP (legit travel / new laptop)
  • DevOps engineer running a plugin-bootstrap script from a CI runner first-time IP
  • Craft CMS CLI plugin install proxied through the web endpoint
  • Site rebuild / restore-from-backup procedures that batch-install plugins
  • Browser-based admin from a corporate VPN egress that rotated
Suppression filter
| where not (UserAgent has_any ("craftcli", "craft-cli", "DeployBot", "GitHub-Hookshot", "Buddy")) and not (SrcIpAddr startswith "10." or SrcIpAddr startswith "192.168." or SrcIpAddr startswith "172.16.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the SrcIpAddr is human-driven (geo, ASN, UA) or programmatic. Look up the user account behind the session via web-app logs and check whether it matches a real admin's recent login from elsewhere (impossible-travel pattern). 2) Contain: if uncorroborated, invalidate Craft CMS Control Panel sessions (rotate session salt), remove any plugin installed within the suspect window from /vendor and database, and block the SrcIpAddr at the edge. 3) Hunt: enumerate all plugins installed in the past 7 days, hash-compare against legitimate Craft plugin store releases, and pivot on the web host for new PHP files, webshells, and scheduled tasks (often the post-install payload from a malicious plugin).
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let BaselineDays = 30d;
let Baseline = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(BaselineDays) .. ago(LookbackHours))
    | where Url has "/admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin" and HttpMethod =~ "POST"
    | summarize BaselineHits = count() by SrcIpAddr
    | where BaselineHits > 0;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
| where Url has "/admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin"
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on SrcIpAddr
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HostHeader = HttpHostName, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, Referer = HttpRequestHeaderReferer, HttpStatusCode, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance scanning of Craft CMS /actions/app/resource-js endpoint AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects external IPs probing the CVE-2026-55791 endpoint at scan-like volume — multiple hits to the resource-js path within a short window, typical of mass internet scanners enumerating vulnerable Craft CMS instances ahead of exploitation. Rationale: Mass scanners (Shodan, Censys, GreyNoise scanners, criminal recon bots) characteristically hit a CVE's known endpoint with 5+ requests/hour from a single source. The 5-hit/1-hour threshold separates them from legitimate admin loads (typically 1-2 hits per CP page view). Excludes RFC1918 to focus on internet-borne scanning. Surfaces method + host-header variation which is the scanner-fingerprint signal. Cross-checked against: • https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10338 • https://dailycve.com/craft-cms-ssrf-via-host-header-cvenot-specified-critical/

Anomalous response size from /actions/app/resource-js (cache-poisoning artefact) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects responses from the Craft CMS resource-js proxy endpoint that are materially larger than the per-environment baseline — the on-wire fingerprint of an attacker-controlled JavaScript payload being served, either fresh from the SSRF or from a poisoned cache. Targets the 'arbitrary JS injection' half of CVE-2026-55791 that request-side detections miss. Rationale: Article §3 says 'the response fetched from the attacker's server is blindly returned to the user' with forced Content-Type: application/javascript. Legitimate Craft resource-js cached responses are tiny (few KB shim wrappers around already-cached asset paths). An attacker delivering a real payload (CSRF-stealer, plugin-installer) inflates the response far beyond baseline — the 2x P95 multiplier is a conservative anti-baseline. Closes the reviewer-flagged gap where request-side detections miss the actual injected payload. Cross-checked against: • https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10338 • https://dailycve.com/craft-cms-ssrf-via-host-header-cvenot-specified-critical/
ATT&CKT1659 T1189 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Craft plugin update changes the resource-js response payload
  • First-time load after a cache flush serving a larger uncompressed payload
  • Craft front-end developer pushing a new larger third-party JS dependency
  • CDN compression disabled briefly during a deploy
  • Sparse baseline (low-traffic site) producing unstable P95
Suppression filter
| where not (HostHeader has_any ("deploy.", "staging.", "-preview.")) and not (HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has "Craft-CMS-Update-Check")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull a sample of the over-sized response (via WAF body capture or replay the URL with the same HostHeader) and inspect the JS for IOC-style indicators: window.Craft.csrfTokenValue extraction, fetch() to /admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin, base64-encoded payload blobs, attacker-controlled exfil URLs. 2) Contain: purge all cache layers (Varnish, Cloudflare, CloudFront) of /actions/app/resource-js entries to evict the poisoned response. Force admins to re-authenticate, rotate CSRF token salt, and freeze plugin installs until patched. 3) Hunt: for each HostHeader value observed in the over-sized responses, search for inbound requests carrying that value as X-Forwarded-Host in the prior 6h to identify the original poisoning request, then pivot on AttackerSrc via UC1.
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let BaselineDays = 30d;
let Baseline = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(BaselineDays) .. ago(LookbackHours))
    | where Url has "/actions/app/resource-js"
    | where HttpStatusCode == 200
    | where isnotempty(HttpResponseBodyBytes)
    | summarize BaselineMedian = percentile(HttpResponseBodyBytes, 50), BaselineP95 = percentile(HttpResponseBodyBytes, 95), BaselineCount = count();
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
| where Url has "/actions/app/resource-js"
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| where isnotempty(HttpResponseBodyBytes)

Crossplane ImageConfig modified to remove cosign signature verification (GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r) AIWeaponization High
Hunts for live edits to Crossplane ImageConfig CRDs that strip or weaken the cosign verification stanza, neutralising the GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r mitigation guidance. Triggers when an UPDATE/PATCH on an imageconfigs.pkg.crossplane.io object lands and the resulting object no longer references cosign/signature verification. Rationale: Article: 'package signature verification to be configured via the ImageConfig mechanism'. Removing or stripping cosign blocks from ImageConfig is the cleanest way to silently bypass the GHSA fix. Single-event, high-confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/concepts/image-configs/
ATT&CKT1562
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Platform engineer migrating from cosign to a different verifier (sigstore policy controller)
  • GitOps reconciliation re-applying a stale manifest that predates the cosign block
  • Cluster upgrade tooling temporarily blanking the spec before re-populating
  • Helm chart upgrade replacing ImageConfig with one that uses a different field name
Suppression filter
| where Username !endswith "-controller" and UserAgent !has "helm" and UserAgent !has "argocd"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the AuditId, diff the prior RequestObject vs the new one, and confirm cosign block was truly removed (vs renamed/migrated). Check Username/UserAgent — was it a human via kubectl or a controller? 2) Contain: re-apply the original ImageConfig from Git/backup; if the actor is a service account, revoke its bind to the pkg.crossplane.io role until reviewed. 3) Hunt: pivot on Username for any subsequent Provider/Configuration/Function installs with tag references (UC3) or skipSignatureVerification=true (UC5) in the next 1h; check whether any packages were installed with verification effectively disabled.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in~ ("update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "imageconfigs.pkg.crossplane.io" or tostring(ObjectRef) has "imageconfigs"
| extend Body = tostring(RequestObject)
| where isnotempty(Body)
| where not(Body matches regex @"(?i)cosign|signatures|verification")
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, RequestUri, ObjectRef, ResponseStatus, UserAgent

Crossplane ImageConfig CRD deletion (signature verification policy removal) AIWeaponization High
Detects deletion of an ImageConfig resource — the policy object that ties packages to cosign verification. Wholesale deletion is the simplest way to disarm signature verification before installing a malicious package, per the GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r mitigation surface. Rationale: Article says verification is configured via ImageConfig. Deleting the CRD instance is a one-call defense-evasion primitive. Article-specific resource name `imageconfigs.pkg.crossplane.io` keeps this from being generic. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/concepts/image-configs/
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cluster decommissioning where the entire pkg.crossplane.io namespace is torn down
  • Operator switching from ImageConfig-based to a new verification mechanism
  • GitOps prune step removing an obsolete ImageConfig that was renamed
  • Test/staging cluster reset scripts
Suppression filter
| where Username !in ("system:serviceaccount:crossplane-system:crossplane", "system:serviceaccount:flux-system:kustomize-controller")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify Username, UserAgent, source IP from AKSAudit; confirm the deletion was not from a controller-loop reconcile. Check whether a replacement ImageConfig was created within the next 5 minutes. 2) Contain: re-apply the deleted ImageConfig from version control; revoke the deleter's RBAC binding to delete pkg.crossplane.io/imageconfigs if not a platform owner. 3) Hunt: search for Provider/Configuration/Function installs by the same Username in the next 60 minutes (UC3) — that's the attack completion step.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb =~ "delete"
| where RequestUri has "imageconfigs.pkg.crossplane.io" or tostring(ObjectRef) has "imageconfigs"
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, RequestUri, ObjectRef, ResponseStatus, UserAgent, AuditId

Crossplane Provider/Configuration/Function installed via mutable tag (no digest) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for Crossplane package installs (Provider/Configuration/Function CRs) that reference an image by mutable tag instead of an immutable @sha256: digest. Per GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r, tag-based installs are the precondition for the TOCTOU; digest-pinned installs are immune. Rationale: Article: 'Installing packages by image digest rather than using tags avoids this issue.' Therefore every tag-based install in a vulnerable cluster is the at-risk population. Hunting tier because tag-based installs are common, but each one is a real exposure to the TOCTOU. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/concepts/packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Initial bootstrap of a cluster where operators are deliberately tag-pinned to a release stream
  • Internal-registry installs from a trusted private registry the team controls
  • Crossplane core demos / lab clusters using upstream :latest
  • GitOps templates that have not yet been digest-pinned by hardening project
Suppression filter
| where Package !startswith "<your-internal-registry-host>/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull spec.package, the source registry, and the installing principal. If the registry is in the team's controlled allow-list (e.g. ECR/ACR in same account), severity drops. 2) Contain: open a ticket to digest-pin the package; if registry is external/uncontrolled, suspend the package (kubectl delete provider/...) and recreate with @sha256:<digest>. 3) Hunt: cross-reference Username + Timestamp against ImageConfig modifications (UC1/UC2) or skipSignatureVerification flag (UC5) — combo = exploit path.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in~ ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has_any ("providers.pkg.crossplane.io","configurations.pkg.crossplane.io","functions.pkg.crossplane.io")
| extend Package = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RequestObject)).spec.package)
| where isnotempty(Package)
| where Package !contains "@sha256:"
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, RequestUri, Package, UserAgent
title: Crossplane Package Installed Via Mutable Tag Reference

Vulnerable Crossplane core version deployed in cluster (GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r affected) AIReconnaissance High
Inventory hunt for clusters running Crossplane core versions affected by GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r: v1.x up to and including 1.21.0-rc.0, v2.2.x ≤ 2.2.2, v2.3.0-rc.0 through 2.3.2. Fixed in v2.3.3 and v2.2.3. Rationale: Article: 'vuln >= 2.3.0-rc.0, <= 2.3.2; vuln <= 2.2.2; vuln <= 1.21.0-rc.0'. Fix shipped in v2.2.3 / v2.3.3. Inventory match against those version ranges is the cleanest exposure signal — every other UC in this set only matters on a vulnerable cluster. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/crossplane/crossplane/releases
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Long-running clusters that have not pulled the v2.2.3 / v2.3.3 fix yet (true positives but operational, not security incidents)
  • Pre-prod clusters intentionally pinned to an older release for compatibility testing
  • Legacy v1.x clusters slated for decommission
  • Bootstrap image pulled momentarily during upgrade transition
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the running version via `kubectl -n crossplane-system get deploy crossplane -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'`. Cross-check the cluster's ImageConfig (is verification even on?) and whether installs use tags (UC3) — only the intersection is exploitable. 2) Contain: schedule upgrade to v2.2.3 / v2.3.3 per release branch; in the interim, switch all package installs to @sha256: digests. 3) Hunt: enumerate Providers/Configurations/Functions referenced by tag on this cluster — those are the at-risk artifacts.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where SoftwareVendor =~ "crossplane" and SoftwareName has "crossplane"
| where SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^(1\.([0-9]|1[0-9]|2[01])\.[0-9]+(-rc\.[0-9]+)?|2\.[0-2]\.[0-2]|2\.3\.[0-2]|2\.3\.0-rc\.[0-9]+)$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, EndOfSupportStatus
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in~ ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has_any ("deployments","pods","providers.pkg.crossplane.io")
| extend Body = tostring(RequestObject)
| where Body has "crossplane/crossplane"
| extend Image = extract(@"crossplane/crossplane[^""]*?:(v?[0-9][^""\s]*)", 1, Body)
| where isnotempty(Image)
| where Image matches regex @"^v?(1\.([0-9]|1[0-9]|2[01])\.[0-9]+(-rc\.[0-9]+)?|2\.[0-2]\.[0-2]|2\.3\.[0-2]|2\.3\.0-rc\.[0-9]+)$"
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, RequestUri, Image

Crossplane skipSignatureVerification bypass flag set on ImageConfig/Provider (GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r) AIWeaponization High
Hunts for explicit `skipSignatureVerification: true` (or equivalent) on Crossplane pkg.crossplane.io resources — a deliberate wholesale bypass of cosign verification that lets an attacker (or insider) install unverified packages without ever needing the TOCTOU race. Rationale: Reviewer-flagged: article explicitly says verification is configured via ImageConfig and is opt-in. A deliberate `skipSignatureVerification: true` is the most direct wholesale-bypass primitive an attacker (or rushed operator) can use to sidestep the GHSA fix entirely. Article-specific resource group `pkg.crossplane.io` keeps this off-the-shelf detection narrow. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r • https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/concepts/image-configs/
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator deliberately disabling verification during cosign key rotation outage
  • Lab/test cluster running unsigned dev packages
  • Bootstrap GitOps step before the cluster's trust roots are populated
  • Air-gapped environment with internal mirror that genuinely cannot fetch upstream signatures
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "flux" and UserAgent !has "argocd" and Username !startswith "system:serviceaccount:crossplane-system:"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull AuditId; review the diff and Username/UserAgent; confirm the flag landed and persisted (re-read the object). Was an exception ticket filed? 2) Contain: patch the resource back to skipSignatureVerification=false (or remove the field); if RBAC permits unjustified self-service of this flag, scope it back to platform-admins via OPA/Gatekeeper policy. 3) Hunt: pivot on Username + Timestamp: any Provider/Configuration/Function install on this cluster in the same window (UC3) is now suspect — verify the installed package against a trusted digest manually.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in~ ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has_any ("imageconfigs.pkg.crossplane.io","providers.pkg.crossplane.io","configurations.pkg.crossplane.io","functions.pkg.crossplane.io")
| extend Body = tostring(RequestObject)
| where Body matches regex @"(?i)skipsignatureverification[""\s:=]+true"
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, RequestUri, ObjectRef, UserAgent, AuditId
title: Crossplane skipSignatureVerification Bypass Flag Set
id: 6b1f0e25-9c3a-4d7e-b820-4e7f1a2b3c55
description: Detects explicit skipSignatureVerification=true on Crossplane pkg.crossplane.io resources, wholesale bypassing cosign verification (GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1562.001
logsource:
  product: kubernetes
  service: audit
detection:
  selection:
    verb:
      - create
      - update
      - patch
    objectRef.apiGroup: pkg.crossplane.io
    objectRef.resource:
      - imageconfigs
      - providers
      - configurations
      - functions
  flag:
    requestObject|re: '(?i)skipsignatureverification["\s:=]+true'
  condition: selection and flag
level: high
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @objectRef.apiGroup:pkg.crossplane.io @objectRef.resource:(imageconfigs OR providers OR configurations OR functions) (@requestObject:*skipSignatureVerification*true* OR @requestObject:*skipsignatureverification*true*)
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count, min(_time) as first_seen, max(_time) as last_seen, values(Change.object_attrs) as attrs from datamodel=Change where Change.object_category="kubernetes_resource" AND Change.object IN ("imageconfigs.pkg.crossplane.io","providers.pkg.crossplane.io","configurations.pkg.crossplane.io","functions.pkg.crossplane.io") AND Change.action IN ("created","updated","modified") by Change.user, Change.object_id, Change.src | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)` | where match(mvjoin(attrs," "), "(?i)skipsignatureverification[\"\s:=]+true")
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as first_seen, max(_time) as last_seen, values(Change.object_attrs) as attrs from datamodel=Change where Change.object_category="kubernetes_resource" AND Change.object IN ("imageconfigs.pkg.crossplane.io","providers.pkg.crossplane.io","configurations.pkg.crossplane.io","functions.pkg.crossplane.io") AND Change.action IN ("created","updated","modified") by Change.user, Change.object_id, Change.src | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)` | where match(mvjoin(attrs," "), "(?i)skipsignatureverification[\"\s:=]+true")
High

15 Malicious JetBrains Plugins Stole AI API Keys from 70,000 Developers

StepSecurity
2026-06-19 10 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A coordinated 8-month supply chain attack planted credential-stealing code inside fake AI coding assistants on the JetBrains Marketplace, quietly exfiltrating OpenAI, DeepSeek, and SiliconFlow API keys to an attacker-controlled server in Beijing -- which our investigation found still operational today.
