Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious JetBrains plugin folder or JAR present in plugins directory · Suspicious browser extension installation · Article-specific behavioural hunt — 15 Malicious JetBrains Plugins Stole AI API Keys from 70,000 Developers
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JetBrains IDE outbound connection to malicious plugin C2 (39.107.60.51) · [LLM] JetBrains IDE plaintext HTTP (port 80) egress to external host · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] HTTP exfil signature: POST to /api/software/ on 39.107.60.51 · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
JetBrains IDE outbound connection to malicious plugin C2 (39.107.60.51) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any JetBrains IDE process (IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm, GoLand, Rider, etc.) establishing an outbound connection to the hardcoded C2 IP 39.107.60.51 used by the 15 malicious plugins disclosed by StepSecurity. Highest-fidelity signal that a developer endpoint has one of the 15 stealer plugins installed — the C2 was confirmed live as of June 19, 2026 (three days after marketplace takedown). Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim C2 IP '39.107.60.51' in the article body + StepSecurity's confirmation the host was still live and serving the '信息管理平台' admin panel three days post-takedown. JetBrains IDE process names are the high-fidelity scope narrower — these binaries should never legitimately reach an Alibaba Cloud Beijing host.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat intel sandbox or malware research VM where an analyst is intentionally detonating one of the plugins
  • Honeypot/canary endpoint emulating a vulnerable developer workstation
  • Pen-test exercise replicating the supply chain attack
  • Defender/CrowdStrike auto-detonation in a cloud sandbox firing real telemetry
  • Internal red team validating coverage against this advisory
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","honeypot","redteam","detonation"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Pull all DeviceNetworkEvents to 39.107.60.51 from this host across the last 240 days. Enumerate %APPDATA%\JetBrains\<IDE>\plugins\ and %LOCALAPPDATA%\JetBrains\<IDE>\plugins\ — look for any of the 15 plugin display names (DeepSeek Junit Test, DeepSeek Git Commit, etc.). 2. CONTAIN: Force IDE restart on the host (JetBrains pushed a kill-switch that disables the plugin on relaunch). Block 39.107.60.51 at egress. Treat every AI provider API key the user ever pasted into any IDE plugin as compromised — rotate OpenAI, DeepSeek, SiliconFlow keys immediately and review billing for unauthorized usage. 3. HUNT: Sweep all developer endpoints for the same plugin directories. Pull AI provider billing/usage logs for unexpected calls from unknown IPs. Check git history for committed API keys with the sk- prefix that could have been re-pasted.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(240d)
| where RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51"
| extend IsJetBrainsIDE = InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("idea64.exe","idea.exe","pycharm64.exe","pycharm.exe","webstorm64.exe","phpstorm64.exe","rubymine64.exe","clion64.exe","goland64.exe","rider64.exe","datagrip64.exe","fleet.exe","studio64.exe","aqua64.exe","rustrover64.exe","dataspell64.exe","mps64.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP, IsJetBrainsIDE
| order by IsJetBrainsIDE desc, Timestamp desc
let C2 = "39.107.60.51";
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(240d)
    | where DstIpAddr == C2
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkBytes, EventVendor, EventProduct, Url),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(240d)
    | where DestinationIP == C2
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname=SourceHostName, SrcUsername=SourceUserName, DstIpAddr=DestinationIP, DstPortNumber=DestinationPort, NetworkBytes=SentBytes, EventVendor=DeviceVendor, EventProduct=DeviceProduct, Url=RequestURL)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: JetBrains IDE Outbound to Malicious Plugin C2 39.107.60.51
id: a3f1e2b4-7c8d-4e5f-9a1b-2c3d4e5f6a7b
description: Detects network connections from JetBrains IDE processes to the C2 IP used by the 15 malicious plugin supply chain attack disclosed by StepSecurity (Jun 2026).
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jetbrains-malicious-plugins-ai-api-key-theft
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1041
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_ide:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\idea64.exe'
      - '\idea.exe'
      - '\pycharm64.exe'
      - '\pycharm.exe'
      - '\webstorm64.exe'
      - '\phpstorm64.exe'
      - '\rubymine64.exe'
      - '\clion64.exe'
      - '\goland64.exe'
      - '\rider64.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high

source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security OR windows.defender OR linux.auditd) (@DestinationIp:39.107.60.51 OR @network.destination.ip:39.107.60.51 OR @RemoteIP:39.107.60.51)
#event_simpleName=/^(NetworkConnectIP4|NetworkConnectIP6)$/ RemoteAddressIP4="39.107.60.51"
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(idea64|idea|pycharm64|pycharm|webstorm64|phpstorm64|rubymine64|clion64|goland64|rider64|datagrip64|fleet|studio64|aqua64|rustrover64|dataspell64|mps64)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count(as=connections))
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="39.107.60.51" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.src_user All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.bytes_out
| `drop_dm_object_name("All_Traffic")`
| eval is_jb_ide=if(match(lower(coalesce(process_name,app,"")),"(idea(64)?|pycharm(64)?|webstorm(64)?|phpstorm(64)?|rubymine(64)?|clion(64)?|goland(64)?|rider(64)?|datagrip(64)?|fleet|studio(64)?|aqua(64)?|rustrover(64)?)\.exe$"),1,0)
| sort - is_jb_ide firstTime

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="39.107.60.51" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.src_user All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.bytes_out
| `drop_dm_object_name("All_Traffic")`
| eval is_jb_ide=if(match(lower(coalesce(process_name,app,"")),"(idea(64)?|pycharm(64)?|webstorm(64)?|phpstorm(64)?|rubymine(64)?|clion(64)?|goland(64)?|rider(64)?|datagrip(64)?|fleet|studio(64)?|aqua(64)?|rustrover(64)?)\.exe$"),1,0)
| sort - is_jb_ide firstTime
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
HTTP exfil signature: POST to /api/software/ on 39.107.60.51 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the verbatim HTTP exfiltration shape used by the 15 malicious plugins — a POST to http://39.107.60.51/api/software/<name> carrying the hardcoded 'X-Api-Key: F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D' header and a JSON body containing the stolen sk- prefixed key. Targets web proxy and ASIM web-session telemetry where URL path and (where available) request headers are visible. Rationale: Three anchored verbatim strings from the article's decompiled BaseUtil.request() snippet: dest IP 39.107.60.51, URL path '/api/software/', and the hardcoded header 'X-Api-Key: F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D'. Any one of those three on the wire is conclusive. The X-Api-Key value in particular is a 20-char custom token with zero possibility of legitimate collision.
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat intel team replaying captured PCAPs through a network sensor
  • Detection engineering team validating signature coverage with a benign test request
  • Sandbox detonation of the malware sample
  • Red team emulating the exfil pattern for purple team exercise
  • Researcher reproducing the attack flow against a controlled lab C2
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Identify the source host. Confirm whether a JetBrains IDE process initiated the request (cross-reference UC1). Capture full URL — the path component after /api/software/ is a campaign-internal identifier. 2. CONTAIN: Block 39.107.60.51 at perimeter. Revoke every AI provider API key the user has touched (OpenAI sk- prefixed keys are the primary target — also DeepSeek and SiliconFlow per article). Force IDE restart to trigger JetBrains' kill-switch. 3. HUNT: Search proxy/firewall logs for any other host that reached 39.107.60.51 or any URL containing '/api/software/' over the past 240 days (campaign ran Oct 2025–Jun 2026). Pull AI provider usage telemetry for unauthorized calls from China-based IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(240d)
| where (RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51" or RemoteUrl has "39.107.60.51")
| where RemotePort == 80 or RemoteUrl has "/api/software/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2 = "39.107.60.51";
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(240d)
    | where DstIpAddr == C2 or Url has C2 or Url has "/api/software/"
    | where HttpMethod == "POST" or isempty(HttpMethod)
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestBodyBytes, EventVendor, EventProduct),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(240d)
    | where DestinationIP == C2 or RequestURL has "39.107.60.51/api/software/"
    | where RequestMethod =~ "POST" or isempty(RequestMethod)
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname=SourceHostName, SrcUsername=SourceUserName, DstIpAddr=DestinationIP, DstPortNumber=DestinationPort, Url=RequestURL, HttpMethod=RequestMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent=RequestClientApplication, HttpRequestBodyBytes=SentBytes, EventVendor=DeviceVendor, EventProduct=DeviceProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious JetBrains plugin folder or JAR present in plugins directory AIInstallation Medium
Hunting query for file-system artefacts of the 15 malicious plugins on developer endpoints — surfaces JAR/folder creations under the JetBrains plugins directory whose name matches one of the 14 disclosed display names or whose plugin ID (org.sm.yms.toolkit, com.json.simple.kit, etc.) appears in path. Helps you find compromised endpoints even after JetBrains' kill-switch has neutered the plugin's execution. Rationale: Anchored on the 14 plugin display names and 14 plugin IDs the article lists verbatim in Table 1. The path predicate \\JetBrains\\...\\plugins\\ narrows scope to the IDE plugins directory which has no legitimate user write activity outside of marketplace installs. Display-name match alone could collide with the legit 'CodeGPT' plugin so we also check plugin IDs which are wholly attacker-controlled and unique.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user installing the legitimate 'CodeGPT' Marketplace plugin (distinct plugin ID — verify against the 14 IDs in the article)
  • Developer rebuilding an IDE config from a backup that pre-dates the JetBrains kill-switch
  • Forensic responder copying the malicious plugin JAR to an analysis VM
  • IDE settings sync from a previously-compromised paired developer machine
  • CI/CD pipeline that bakes IDE installations into golden images and tests one of these names
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\quarantine\\","\\malware-samples\\","\\forensics\\","\\sandbox\\"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Confirm the file path is under a real JetBrains plugins directory (not a quarantine/sample folder). Inventory which plugin ID(s) hit — cross-reference Table 1 of the article to identify which malicious plugin. Capture file hash. 2. CONTAIN: Force restart of the JetBrains IDE on the host (triggers JetBrains' remote kill-switch). Delete the offending plugin folder. Treat any AI provider key the user has used (OpenAI, DeepSeek, SiliconFlow) as compromised: rotate immediately and audit provider billing/usage for unauthorized calls. 3. HUNT: Sweep developer fleet for any of the 14 display names or 14 plugin IDs in plugins directories. Pivot on the user's git history for accidentally committed sk- keys. Check 39.107.60.51 connection history per UC1 to identify which keys were actually exfiltrated.
let bad_display_names = dynamic(["DeepSeek Junit Test","DeepSeek Git Commit","DeepSeek FindBugs","DeepSeek AI Chat","DeepSeek Dev AI","DeepSeek AI Coding","AI FindBugs","AI Git Commitor","AI Coder Review","DeepSeek Coder AI","AI Coder Assistant","DeepSeek Code Review","CodeGPT AI Assistant","DeepSeek AI Assist"]);
let bad_plugin_ids = dynamic(["org.sm.yms.toolkit","com.json.simple.kit","org.bug.find.tools","org.translate.ai.simple","com.yy.test.ai.simple","com.dev.ai.toolkit","com.json.view.simple","com.my.git.ai.kit","org.check.ai.ds","com.review.tool.code","org.code.assist.dev.tool","com.coder.ai.dpt","com.my.code.tools","ord.cp.code.ai.kit"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(240d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has @"\JetBrains\" and FolderPath has @"\plugins\"
| where FolderPath has_any (bad_display_names) or FileName has_any (bad_display_names) or FolderPath has_any (bad_plugin_ids) or FileName has_any (bad_plugin_ids)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileSize
| order by Timestamp desc
let bad_display_names = dynamic(["DeepSeek Junit Test","DeepSeek Git Commit","DeepSeek FindBugs","DeepSeek AI Chat","DeepSeek Dev AI","DeepSeek AI Coding","AI FindBugs","AI Git Commitor","AI Coder Review","DeepSeek Coder AI","AI Coder Assistant","DeepSeek Code Review","CodeGPT AI Assistant","DeepSeek AI Assist"]);
let bad_plugin_ids = dynamic(["org.sm.yms.toolkit","com.json.simple.kit","org.bug.find.tools","org.translate.ai.simple","com.yy.test.ai.simple","com.dev.ai.toolkit","com.json.view.simple","com.my.git.ai.kit","org.check.ai.ds","com.review.tool.code","org.code.assist.dev.tool","com.coder.ai.dpt","com.my.code.tools","ord.cp.code.ai.kit"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(240d)
| where TargetFilePath has "JetBrains" and TargetFilePath has "plugins"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (bad_display_names) or TargetFileName has_any (bad_display_names) or TargetFilePath has_any (bad_plugin_ids) or TargetFileName has_any (bad_plugin_ids)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JetBrains IDE plaintext HTTP (port 80) egress to external host AICommand & Control Medium
Behavioural hunt for the defense-evasion technique flagged in the article — the malicious plugins installed a JVM-wide X509TrustManager to suppress TLS warnings, then exfiltrated over plaintext HTTP on port 80 to dodge TLS-inspection telemetry. Legitimate JetBrains IDE traffic is overwhelmingly HTTPS (Marketplace, update channels, license check); a JetBrains IDE making port-80 outbound to a public IP is a strong anomaly signal that catches this campaign and future copycats that retain the plaintext-HTTP exfil pattern with a different IP. Rationale: Article explicitly calls out the TLS warning suppression + plaintext HTTP (port 80) exfil as a deliberate evasion choice: 'while it makes interception trivial for network defenders, it also means the attacker avoided the complexity of managing TLS certificates.' Legitimate JetBrains traffic — Marketplace, updates, license check — is HTTPS, so port-80 JetBrains egress to public IPs is a strong anomaly. Excludes jetbrains.com/intellij.net to suppress the few legitimate HTTP redirects.
ATT&CKT1573 T1071.001 T1562.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped/on-prem artifact repo (Nexus, Artifactory) serving Gradle/Maven dependencies over HTTP
  • Internal license server reachable only over HTTP
  • Developer manually pointing the IDE at an HTTP-only test API while debugging
  • Corporate proxy auto-config script forcing HTTP for certain destinations
  • First-launch IDE telemetry that briefly hits an HTTP captive-portal check
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP in ("10.","172.16.","172.17.","172.18.","172.19.","172.20.","172.21.","172.22.","172.23.","172.24.","172.25.","172.26.","172.27.","172.28.","172.29.","172.30.","172.31.","192.168.") or RemoteUrl has_any ("artifactory","nexus","jfrog","sonatype"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: For each src→dst pair, resolve the dst IP — is it a known corporate Maven/Nexus/Artifactory server? If yes, allowlist. If unknown / external, treat as suspicious. Pull the IDE log at %APPDATA%\JetBrains\<IDE>\log\idea.log for plugin load entries around the connection time. 2. CONTAIN: If the dst IP matches 39.107.60.51 or any other suspicious external host, follow the UC1 containment workflow (rotate API keys, force IDE restart, block egress). 3. HUNT: Pivot on the dst IP — has any other developer endpoint reached it? Run UC3 (file detection) on the host to see which plugin was installed. Look for any X-Api-Key headers on the dst connection if proxy header logging is on.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("idea64.exe","idea.exe","pycharm64.exe","pycharm.exe","webstorm64.exe","phpstorm64.exe","rubymine64.exe","clion64.exe","goland64.exe","rider64.exe","datagrip64.exe","fleet.exe","studio64.exe","aqua64.exe","rustrover64.exe","dataspell64.exe")
| where RemotePort == 80
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("jetbrains.com","intellij.net","plugins.jetbrains.com"))
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), ConnCount = count(), SampleUrls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 5) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
let JBIDEs = dynamic(["idea64.exe","idea.exe","pycharm64.exe","pycharm.exe","webstorm64.exe","phpstorm64.exe","rubymine64.exe","clion64.exe","goland64.exe","rider64.exe","datagrip64.exe","fleet.exe","studio64.exe","aqua64.exe","rustrover64.exe"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstPortNumber == 80
| extend ParentBin = tostring(split(tolower(SrcUsername),"\\")[-1])
| where SrcHostname has_any (JBIDEs) or ParentBin in (JBIDEs)
| where not (Url has_any ("jetbrains.com","intellij.net"))
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), ConnCount = count(), SampleUrls = make_set(Url, 5) by SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\idea64.exe OR *\\idea.exe OR *\\pycharm64.exe OR *\\webstorm64.exe OR *\\phpstorm64.exe OR *\\rubymine64.exe OR *\\clion64.exe OR *\\goland64.exe OR *\\rider64.exe OR *\\datagrip64.exe OR *\\fleet.exe OR *\\studio64.exe OR *\\IDEA64.exe OR *\\PyCharm64.exe) @DestinationPort:80 -@DestinationHostname:*jetbrains.com -@DestinationHostname:*intellij.net
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=80
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(idea64|idea|pycharm64|pycharm|webstorm64|phpstorm64|rubymine64|clion64|goland64|rider64|datagrip64|fleet|studio64|aqua64|rustrover64|dataspell64)\.exe$/i
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4) | NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4) | NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4], function={ count(as=conns) | min(_time, as=firstSeen) | max(_time, as=lastSeen) })

| eval is_jb_ide=if(match(lower(coalesce(process_name,app,"")),"(idea(64)?|pycharm(64)?|webstorm(64)?|phpstorm(64)?|rubymine(64)?|clion(64)?|goland(64)?|rider(64)?|datagrip(64)?|fleet|studio(64)?|aqua(64)?|rustrover(64)?)\.exe$"),1,0)

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.

Gravity SMTP WordPress plugin info-disclosure exploit (CVE-2026-4020) AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated GET requests to the vulnerable Gravity SMTP REST endpoint /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data, which returns a JSON System Report containing live SES, Google, Mailjet, Resend and Zoho API credentials when the plugin is <= 2.1.4. Wordfence reports 17M+ blocked attempts against this exact path with a 4M-request spike on June 7, 2026, so a single successful (HTTP 200) response is a credential-compromise event. Rationale: Anchored on the two article-specific IOCs Defiant/Wordfence published: the REST path /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data and the ?page=gravitysmtp-settings query parameter (the latter distinguishes automated exploit tooling from opportunistic probing). The detection separates Attempts from Successes (HTTP 200) so the SOC can prioritise the small subset where the System Report was actually returned and credentials need rotating. Defender, Datadog standard sources, Falcon EDR and CloudWatch are intentionally empty: this is a server-side web-access-log detection and none of those telemetry layers see inbound WordPress HTTP requests in a default deployment. No external corroboration searched — the Bleeping Computer article cites the primary Wordfence/Defiant advisory and the IOC strings are unambiguous.
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001 T1589.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised external vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Tenable.io, Burp Suite) probing the endpoint within an approved scope — typically high attempts, no Successes
  • Wordfence / WPScan post-patch verification scans hitting every known-vulnerable plugin path
  • Internal blue/purple team patch-validation hitting the path from a corporate jump host or VPN egress IP
  • SRE / support engineers pulling the System Report through the admin UI for troubleshooting — originates from an authenticated admin session via the wp-admin POST path, not direct GET to the REST endpoint
  • Mass-Internet scanners (Censys, Shodan, ShadowServer) opportunistically probing /wp-json/* — usually distinguishable by hitting many other plugins' REST routes in the same window
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in (dynamic(["<authorised-scanner-IP>", "<internal-jumphost-IP>"]))
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "Wordfence" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "WPScan" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "Nessus" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "Qualys"
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm `Successes` > 0 for the SrcIpAddr; a single 200 means the JSON System Report (SES/Google/Mailjet/Resend/Zoho API keys, DB table names, plugin inventory, PHP env) was exfiltrated. Pull the response size from WAF/proxy logs to verify a real payload (typically several KB). Cross-reference the target site's installed Gravity SMTP version against 2.1.5. 2) Contain — immediately upgrade Gravity SMTP to >= 2.1.5 on every affected site, then rotate every credential the plugin had configured: AWS SES access-key pairs, Google service-account tokens / OAuth refresh tokens, Mailjet / Resend / Zoho API keys, and any plain-SMTP passwords. Block the SrcIpAddr at the WAF/CDN and add to the org IP blocklist; pull all WP REST endpoints in the same time window to catch lateral plugin probing. 3) Hunt — query AWS CloudTrail SES SendEmail / SendRawEmail / SendBulkTemplatedEmail and Google Workspace mailflow audit logs for unauthorised sends in the 48h after the first successful exfil;
let lookback = 7d;
// ASIM web-session view normalises IIS, Apache, Nginx, F5, Azure App Gateway and most WAFs.
// If ASIM parsers are not enabled, swap ImWebSession for W3CIISLog / AzureDiagnostics / CommonSecurityLog.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Url has "/wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data"
| extend HasSettingsParam = Url has "page=gravitysmtp-settings"
| extend StatusCode = coalesce(HttpResponseCode, HttpStatusCode)
| summarize
    Attempts    = count(),
    Successes   = countif(StatusCode == 200),                // 200 = System Report exfiltrated
    Blocked     = countif(StatusCode between (400 .. 599)),
    FirstSeen   = min(TimeGenerated),
    LastSeen    = max(TimeGenerated),
    TargetSites = dcount(DstHostname),
    SitesList   = make_set(DstHostname, 20),
    SampleUA    = any(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent),
    SampleUrl   = any(Url)
    by SrcIpAddr, HasSettingsParam
| extend Severity = case(Successes > 0, "High",
                         HasSettingsParam and Attempts >= 5, "Medium",
                         "Low")
| order by Successes desc, Attempts desc

GentleKiller BYOVD vulnerable-driver file drop (Kaspersky/FACEIT/Valorant/Javelin/etc.) AIInstallation High
Detect file creation of the eight vulnerable/malicious driver filenames the GentleKiller framework uses for BYOVD EDR-killing. Each variant impersonates a different security vendor but drops one of a fixed driver-name set; the names themselves are distinctive enough that a write event on any modern endpoint is high-fidelity for Gentlemen RaaS pre-encryption activity. Rationale: Driver filenames are pulled verbatim from the ESET report block listing the eight GentleKiller variants. These names (especially '360netmon_wfp.sys','IMFForceDelete.sys','PoisonX.sys','stpm_old.sys') are not Microsoft-shipped Windows drivers, so a file-create event for any of them outside DriverStore is highly suspicious. PoisonX.sys is cross-corroborated by Huntress per the article. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/the-gentlemen-raas-uses-gentlekiller.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Kaspersky product install staging eb.sys outside of DriverStore (rare on enterprise endpoints)
  • Game integrity research labs unpacking Valorant or FACEIT installers and dropping GameDriverX64.sys / nseckrnl.sys
  • Security researcher detonating a public GentleKiller PoC in a sandbox VM
  • Backup/forensic tools copying driver files to evidence shares
  • Driver-signing test harness on a developer workstation
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"C:\Program Files\Kaspersky Lab\", @"C:\Riot Games\VALORANT\", @"C:\Program Files (x86)\FACEIT AC\") and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName in~ ("Kaspersky Lab","Riot Games, Inc.","FACEIT LTD"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on InitiatingProcessFileName + InitiatingProcessCommandLine — if the writer is not a vendor installer (e.g. KasperskySetup.exe, MsiExec.exe with a known package) it is almost certainly malicious. Cross-check SHA256 against VT/ESET and collect the file. 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender 'Isolate device' or EDR equivalent; revoke the user's session tokens; check for the matching service entry under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\ and delete only after collection. 3) Hunt: search org-wide for the same SHA256/SHA1, for sibling driver names from the other 7 variants, for parallel writes of OxideHarvest artifacts, and for service-control-manager EID 7045 entries referencing the dropped .sys file in the previous 24h.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName in~ ("eb.sys","nseckrnl.sys","GameDriverX64.sys","stpm_old.sys","stpm_new.sys","dmx.sys","360netmon_wfp.sys","IMFForceDelete.sys","PoisonX.sys")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where not(FolderPath has @"C:\Windows\System32\DriverStore\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,

          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TargetFileName in~ ("eb.sys","nseckrnl.sys","GameDriverX64.sys","stpm_old.sys","stpm_new.sys","dmx.sys","360netmon_wfp.sys","IMFForceDelete.sys","PoisonX.sys")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where not(TargetFilePath has @"C:\Windows\System32\DriverStore\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA1, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

| where NOT match(file_path,"(?i)C:\\\\Windows\\\\System32\\\\DriverStore\\\\")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
GentleKiller / EDR-killer driver service registration in CurrentControlSet\Services AIInstallation High
BYOVD attacks must register the vulnerable driver as a kernel service before invoking it. Detect Services\ key creation or ImagePath set referencing the eight GentleKiller driver names, the three external killers (HexKiller, ThrottleBlood, HavocKiller), or hrwfpdrv.sys. This catches the variant where the file lands under a renamed path but the service name still matches. Rationale: Article enumerates the exact driver filenames and explicitly notes BYOVD operationalization within days of PoC disclosure — service registration is the next step after dropping the .sys. Includes 'hrwfpdrv.sys' which the Huntress write-up cited inside the article paired with PoisonX.sys during a BeyondTrust-Remote-Support intrusion. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/the-gentlemen-raas-uses-gentlekiller.html
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Kaspersky AV install genuinely registering eb.sys service on a managed endpoint
  • Riot Vanguard installing GameDriverX64.sys on a corporate dev/gaming machine
  • FACEIT anti-cheat installer on QA gaming rigs registering nseckrnl.sys
  • Driver-signing CI pipelines that register test drivers under CurrentControlSet\Services
  • Backup-and-restore of a system image that replays old service entries
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName in~ ("Kaspersky Lab","AO Kaspersky Lab","Riot Games, Inc.","FACEIT LTD","Microsoft Corporation") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"C:\Program Files\", @"C:\Program Files (x86)\", @"C:\Windows\Installer\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the user/process registering the service is a legitimate vendor installer (signed parent, MSI/Setup binary in Program Files). Pull the dropped .sys SHA256 and submit to ESET/VT — match against the 20 SHA1 IOCs the article ships. 2) Contain: stop the kernel service (`sc stop <name>`) before deleting, then isolate the host. Block the SHA256 at endpoint policy. Reset the registering account's credentials — Gentlemen affiliates typically drop the killer from an already-elevated session. 3) Hunt: pivot the LogonId/session to find every other process in that session in the previous 60 minutes; query for sibling drivers; look for OxideHarvest browser-profile reads; check VSS/shadow-copy deletion; sweep for vendor-impersonation file metadata (CompanyName matching ESET/Kaspersky/Microsoft on non-vendor binaries).
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("eb.sys","nseckrnl.sys","GameDriverX64.sys","stpm_old.sys","stpm_new.sys","dmx.sys","360netmon_wfp.sys","IMFForceDelete.sys","PoisonX.sys","googleApiUtil64.sys","ThrottleBlood.sys","havoc.sys","hrwfpdrv.sys")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("services.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where EventID in (4697, 7045)
    | extend SvcName = extract(@"(?i)Service Name:\s*([^\r\n]+)", 1, EventData)
    | extend SvcFile = extract(@"(?i)Service File Name:\s*([^\r\n]+)", 1, EventData)
    | where SvcFile has_any ("eb.sys","nseckrnl.sys","GameDriverX64.sys","stpm_old.sys","stpm_new.sys","dmx.sys","360netmon_wfp.sys","IMFForceDelete.sys","PoisonX.sys","googleApiUtil64.sys","ThrottleBlood.sys","havoc.sys","hrwfpdrv.sys")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, SubjectUserName, SvcName, SvcFile),
  (ImRegistryEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
    | where RegistryValue =~ "ImagePath"
    | where RegistryValueData has_any ("eb.sys","nseckrnl.sys","GameDriverX64.sys","stpm_old.sys","stpm_new.sys","dmx.sys","360netmon_wfp.sys","IMFForceDelete.sys","PoisonX.sys","googleApiUtil64.sys","ThrottleBlood.sys","havoc.sys","hrwfpdrv.sys")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValueData,
              ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine)

Third-party EDR-killer driver image load (HexKiller / ThrottleBlood / HavocKiller / hrwfpdrv) AIInstallation High
Detect kernel-mode image loads of the third-party BYOVD drivers ESET observed The Gentlemen affiliates pulling in alongside GentleKiller: googleApiUtil64.sys (HexKiller, previously Warlock-exclusive), ThrottleBlood.sys (MedusaLocker/DragonForce), havoc.sys (HavocKiller/HwAudKiller), and hrwfpdrv.sys (paired with PoisonX in the Huntress-cited BeyondTrust intrusion). These names are distinctive third-party tooling — not legitimate Microsoft/Google drivers — so any image-load is alert-grade. Rationale: Filenames pulled verbatim from the ESET 'third-party BYOVD-based EDR killers' block in the article. The name 'googleApiUtil64.sys' is impersonation - no Google driver exists by that name - so a load is unambiguous; same with 'ThrottleBlood.sys' which is corroborated by ESET via MedusaLocker/DragonForce sightings. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/the-gentlemen-raas-uses-gentlekiller.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst loading a captured sample in a lab VM
  • Reverse-engineering team running IDA/x64dbg against the driver in a sandbox
  • Incident response engagement importing IOCs into a forensic image for offline review
  • Security training lab demonstrating BYOVD techniques
  • Internal red-team exercise using the same tools (should be pre-authorised)
Response runbook
1) Triage: image-load alone means the kernel accepted the driver - so the host is already compromised at SYSTEM/kernel level. Pull running services (`sc query`) and `fltmc filters` to find the registered filter; correlate the loading process's parent chain for the initial-access vector. 2) Contain: physically isolate the host (network isolation may be insufficient once a kernel filter is loaded). Reimage rather than clean - kernel persistence at this level is not safely remediable in-place. Revoke any privileged credentials known to have used the host. 3) Hunt: search for the four driver names across the fleet; sweep for the GentleKiller driver names (UC1); look for vssadmin/wmic shadow-copy deletion in the next 24h and OxideHarvest browser-profile reads; check BeyondTrust Remote Support session logs around the same window per the Huntress reference.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("googleApiUtil64.sys","ThrottleBlood.sys","havoc.sys","hrwfpdrv.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 6
| extend ImageLoaded = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).DataItem.EventData.Data[3].["#text"])
| where ImageLoaded has_any ("googleApiUtil64.sys","ThrottleBlood.sys","havoc.sys","hrwfpdrv.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ImageLoaded, EventData

OxideHarvest stealer reading credential stores across niche browser portfolio (Torch/Comodo/Epic/BlackHawk/IceCat) AIActions on Objectives High
OxideHarvest (aka buildx641) is a Rust stealer ESET ties to the Gentlemen ecosystem that targets a distinctive long-tail browser list - including very niche browsers (Torch, Comodo Dragon, Epic Privacy Browser, Waterfox, BlackHawk, IceCat) that almost no legitimate enterprise software touches. Detect a single non-browser process touching credential stores across MULTIPLE of these niche browser profile paths within a short window. Rationale: Browser list pulled verbatim from the ESET-attributed OxideHarvest section. Targeting niche browsers like Torch, Comodo Dragon, Epic Privacy, BlackHawk and IceCat is the distinguishing feature - enterprise tools (MFA brokers, password sync clients) don't touch these. A non-browser process reading credential SQLite files across two or more of them is essentially a Rust-stealer signature. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/the-gentlemen-raas-uses-gentlekiller.html
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise password manager (LastPass/1Password/Bitwarden) import wizard reading Chrome/Edge/Brave Login Data during onboarding
  • Browser-migration utility on a freshly imaged endpoint copying profiles between Vivaldi/Brave/Opera
  • Endpoint backup agent (Code42/CrashPlan) indexing AppData
  • Forensic tool (FTK Imager, X-Ways) imaging a user profile during IR
  • DLP scanner inspecting AppData looking for credentials at rest
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductName has_any ("LastPass","1Password","Bitwarden","Dashlane","Keeper","NordPass","BrowserMigration","ImportFromBrowser"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess SHA256 and parent chain. Check digital signature - OxideHarvest is Rust-compiled and unsigned. Cross-reference SHA1 against the 20 hashes ESET shipped (article pre-extracted IOCs). 2) Contain: isolate device, force-rotate ALL stored browser passwords for the affected user (treat both work and personal accounts as compromised - browsers do not respect that boundary), invalidate refresh tokens / Entra sign-in sessions, and revoke any session cookies the stealer may have grabbed. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound network from the same process to find the OxideHarvest exfil endpoint; sweep org-wide for the same SHA256; check whether the same host shows GentleKiller driver activity (UC1/UC2) - OxideHarvest often runs alongside in Gentlemen intrusions per ESET.
let NicheBrowserStores = dynamic([@"\Torch\User Data\", @"\Comodo\Dragon\User Data\", @"\Epic Privacy Browser\", @"\Waterfox\Profiles\", @"\NETGATE Technologies\BlackHawk\", @"\Mozilla\IceCat\", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\", @"\Vivaldi\User Data\", @"\Opera Software\Opera GX Stable\", @"\Opera Software\Opera Stable\"]);
let CredFiles = dynamic(["Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","logins.json","key4.db","cookies.sqlite","places.sqlite"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ (CredFiles)
| where FolderPath has_any (NicheBrowserStores)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","waterfox.exe","icecat.exe","dragon.exe","torch.exe","epic.exe","operagx.exe","blackhawk.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize StoresTouched = dcount(strcat(tostring(array_index_of(NicheBrowserStores, tostring(extract("(\\\\[^\\\\]+\\\\(?:User Data|Profiles)\\\\)", 1, FolderPath))))),
            PathsTouched = make_set(FolderPath, 25),
            FilesTouched = make_set(FileName, 25),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            Reads = count()
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where StoresTouched >= 2 or Reads >= 5
| order by LastSeen desc
let NicheBrowserStores = dynamic([@"\Torch\User Data\", @"\Comodo\Dragon\User Data\", @"\Epic Privacy Browser\", @"\Waterfox\Profiles\", @"\NETGATE Technologies\BlackHawk\", @"\Mozilla\IceCat\", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\", @"\Vivaldi\User Data\", @"\Opera Software\Opera GX Stable\", @"\Opera Software\Opera Stable\"]);

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize Reads = count(),
            PathsTouched = make_set(TargetFilePath, 25),
            FilesTouched = make_set(TargetFileName, 25),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where Reads >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc

Mass termination of EDR/AV processes consistent with GentleKiller's 400-process target list AIActions on Objectives Medium
GentleKiller enumerates and terminates 400 processes across 48 distinct security vendor product lines. Hunt for any single process that issues kills (taskkill, Stop-Process, NtTerminateProcess) against a high count of well-known EDR/AV/XDR processes within a short window. Threshold-based with empirical justification. Rationale: Threshold of 5+ distinct EDR processes targeted within 5 minutes is empirically grounded in ESET's '400 processes / 48 vendors' figure - legitimate uninstallers touch one product family, not five. Process list pulled from major vendor product naming (Defender/CrowdStrike/SentinelOne/ESET/Kaspersky/McAfee/Symantec/Trend/FireEye/Cylance/Carbon Black/Sophos/Tanium/Trend/Bitdefender/360/Qihoo). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/the-gentlemen-raas-uses-gentlekiller.html
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1489
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV-product changeover (uninstalling McAfee + installing CrowdStrike) where IT runs a cleanup script
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting a misbehaving EDR sensor with sequential `sc stop`/`Stop-Service` from a labelled admin session
  • Image-build pipeline removing legacy security tooling before sysprep
  • Legitimate uninstaller (e.g. CrowdStrike CsUninstallTool) that iterates services
  • Forensic IR tool that pauses security agents to capture memory (RECon/EnCase)
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("CsUninstallTool.exe","CSSensorRemover.exe","mcafeeendpointassistant.exe","frminst.exe","SophosUninstaller.exe") and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("CrowdStrike","McAfee","Sophos","SentinelOne","Microsoft Corporation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and its grandparent. If parent is services.exe + signed Microsoft binary, likely benign. If parent is a one-off binary in %TEMP%, %ProgramData%, or AppData, treat as confirmed. Pull the binary hash; cross-check against the 20 SHA1 IOCs. 2) Contain: isolate device, kill the calling process tree, revoke session, and verify that AV/EDR has actually been disabled by re-enrolling the sensor agent. 3) Hunt: in the same session, look for BYOVD driver drop (UC1) or driver service registration (UC2) - GentleKiller always pairs the kill with a kernel driver because user-mode taskkill alone won't stop a tamper-protected EDR. Sweep the fleet for the same source binary's SHA256 and for the affiliate's lateral-movement footprint (RDP / SMB) in the prior 4 hours.
let EdrProcessTargets = dynamic(["MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","SenseCncProxy.exe","CSFalconService.exe","CSFalconContainer.exe","CSAgent.exe","SentinelAgent.exe","SentinelHelperService.exe","SentinelStaticEngine.exe","ekrn.exe","egui.exe","avp.exe","avpui.exe","ksde.exe","klnagent.exe","mfemms.exe","mcshield.exe","ccSvcHst.exe","SymCorpUI.exe","xagt.exe","CylanceSvc.exe","CylanceUI.exe","RepMgr.exe","cb.exe","CarbonBlackK.exe","sophos*","SAVService.exe","HxTsr.exe","TaniumClient.exe","ds_agent.exe","ds_monitor.exe","BDAgent.exe","vsserv.exe","PccNTMon.exe","tmccsf.exe","360tray.exe","QHSafeTray.exe","rphcp.exe","WRSA.exe","WSSecuritySvc.exe","PaloAltoNetworks*","Traps.exe","cyserver.exe"]);
let Window = 5m;
let TerminateCmds = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ ("taskkill.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","sc.exe","wmic.exe")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("taskkill","Stop-Process","Stop-Service"," stop ","NtTerminateProcess","TerminateProcess")
    | mv-expand Target = EdrProcessTargets
    | where ProcessCommandLine has tostring(Target)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
              InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              KillerCmd = ProcessCommandLine, Target = tostring(Target)
    | summarize DistinctEdrTargets = dcount(Target), TargetSamples = make_set(Target, 50),
                CmdSamples = make_set(KillerCmd, 10),
                FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
                by DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId,
                   bin(Timestamp, Window)
    | where DistinctEdrTargets >= 5;
let HandleOpens = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("OpenProcessApiCall","ProcessPrimaryTokenModified")
    | where FileName in~ (EdrProcessTargets)
    | summarize DistinctEdrTargets = dcount(FileName),
                Handles = count(),
                TargetSamples = make_set(FileName, 50),
                FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
                by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId,
                   InitiatingProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, Window)
    | where DistinctEdrTargets >= 10;
union TerminateCmds, HandleOpens
| order by LastSeen desc
let EdrProcessTargets = dynamic(["MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","CSFalconService.exe","CSAgent.exe","SentinelAgent.exe","SentinelHelperService.exe","ekrn.exe","egui.exe","avp.exe","ksde.exe","mfemms.exe","mcshield.exe","ccSvcHst.exe","SymCorpUI.exe","xagt.exe","CylanceSvc.exe","cb.exe","CarbonBlackK.exe","SAVService.exe","HxTsr.exe","TaniumClient.exe","ds_agent.exe","BDAgent.exe","PccNTMon.exe","360tray.exe","QHSafeTray.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("taskkill.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sc.exe","net.exe","wmic.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("taskkill","Stop-Process","Stop-Service","NtTerminateProcess","TerminateProcess"," stop ")
| extend HitTargets = set_intersect(EdrProcessTargets, extract_all(@"([A-Za-z0-9_.+-]+\.exe)", CommandLine))
| extend DistinctEdrTargets = array_length(HitTargets)
| where DistinctEdrTargets >= 5
| summarize Window = make_set(TimeGenerated, 10), Targets = make_set(HitTargets), Cmds = make_set(CommandLine, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count()
            by Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @CommandLine:(*taskkill* OR *Stop-Process* OR *Stop-Service* OR *NtTerminateProcess* OR *TerminateProcess*) @CommandLine:(*MsMpEng* OR *MsSense* OR *CSFalcon* OR *CSAgent* OR *SentinelAgent* OR *ekrn* OR *egui* OR *avp.exe* OR *ksde* OR *mfemms* OR *mcshield* OR *ccSvcHst* OR *SymCorpUI* OR *xagt* OR *CylanceSvc* OR *CarbonBlack* OR *sophos* OR *HxTsr* OR *TaniumClient* OR *ds_agent* OR *BDAgent* OR *PccNTMon* OR *360tray* OR *QHSafeTray*)

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-26125")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-26125")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-26125")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-26125")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

DeviceProcessEvents

status: experimental

    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that

references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/

author: Clankerusecase

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "ba914fe77b177b45799403b16dd14765c510a074", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive hash match
level: critical

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Steer the agent to load an attacker's web page, and that page's JavaScript can reach a privileged local service on the same machine and spawn a process on the host. No credentials, no sign-in screen, and no further user interaction once
